summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — removal, reasonable-efforts, and permanency requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of placement decisions

New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Answering certified questions from the Second Circuit, the Court of Appeals held that a child's exposure to domestic violence does not alone establish neglect or justify removal, that neglect requires a preponderance showing of actual or imminent impairment caused by the parent's failure to exercise a minimum degree of care, and that emergency removal without a court order under Family Court Act § 1024 is permissible only where the danger is so urgent that there is no time to obtain an ex parte order.
key_cases.relevance: Foster placement must rest on particularized evidence of imminent risk and on the balance between the harm of remaining home and the harm of removal.
key_cases.quote: emergency removal is appropriate where the danger is so immediate, so urgent that the child's life or safety will be at risk before an ex parte order can be obtained

key_cases.holding: The Court held that awarding custody to foster parents under Social Services Law § 392(6) was impermissible and that the best-interests inquiry for a child in temporary foster care compares continued foster care against discharge to the biological parent or other relative or suitable person, rather than measuring parent against foster parent.
key_cases.relevance: Foster care is characterized as a temporary way station, not a permanent condition or a competing custodial claim.
key_cases.quote: analysis of the child's "best interest" must begin not by measuring biological parent against foster parent but by weighing past and continued foster care against discharge to the biological parent

key_cases.case_name: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that without deciding whether foster parents have a constitutionally protected liberty interest, New York's pre-removal procedures under Social Services Law § 392 and New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate to protect any such interest.
key_cases.relevance: This decision defines the limited procedural rights that attach when a child is moved between foster placements in New York.
key_cases.quote: the procedures provided by New York State in § 392 and by New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate to protect whatever liberty interests appellees may have

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Appellate Division, the Court held that a municipality that assumes legal custody of a child by placing the child in foster care owes that child a common-law duty of care, so the plaintiff need not plead or prove a special duty to sue for negligent selection, retention, or supervision of the foster home.
key_cases.relevance: Placing a child in foster care creates an affirmative, enforceable duty of care owed by the placing municipality.
key_cases.quote: municipalities owe a duty of care to the children the municipalities place in foster homes because the municipalities have assumed custody of those children
